title: What an issue is
blurb: Define an issue the APM way: a problem breaching delegated tolerances that needs the sponsor.
question: A project manager has authority to absorb up to two weeks of delay. A supplier collapse has just caused a six-week delay, while a painter's two-day absence was recovered within float. Which of these is an 'issue' in APM terms, and why?

teach.h: An issue is a problem beyond your limits
teach.body: APM defines an issue as a problem that is now breaching, or is about to breach, the delegated tolerances for work on a project, and that needs the sponsor's support to agree a resolution. In plain English: something has gone wrong, it is bigger than the limits the project manager was trusted to handle alone, so the sponsor must help decide what to do.

items.label: It has happened or is happening: certain, not uncertain
It breaches, or is about to breach, delegated tolerances
It needs the sponsor's support to agree a resolution

teach.caption: Miss any one of the three and it is not an issue in the APM sense.

teach.body: When the sponsor appoints a project manager, they agree limits within which the PM may manage without asking permission: for example, the finish date may move by up to two weeks, or costs by up to £10,000. These permitted deviations are the delegated tolerances. Inside them, the project manager simply sorts problems out. Outside them, the decision belongs to the sponsor.

teach.caption: Tolerance here is plus or minus £10k. A forecast of £214k breaches it, so it is an issue for the sponsor.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Harbourside Medical Centre fit-out
teach.body: The sponsor gives the PM a schedule tolerance of two weeks. On Monday a plasterer is off sick for two days; the PM moves the work into float and the end date holds. That is a day-to-day problem, not an issue. On Thursday the flooring supplier goes into administration and the replacement can't deliver for six weeks. That breaches the tolerance, so it is an issue: the PM must take it to the sponsor.

You don't wait for the damage to land. If a forecast shows a tolerance will be breached, the problem is already an issue and should be raised straight away, while the sponsor still has the most options. Escalating early is good management, not panic. Waiting until the money has actually been overspent leaves fewer and costlier choices.

teach.h: Who deals with a problem depends on its size

levels.label: Team member: within their work package

teach.caption: Each level handles what fits inside its tolerance and escalates what doesn't.

rows.label: Has it happened?
values: Yes, or a breach is imminent

teach.text: Two wrong definitions the exam loves: 'a problem that occurs day to day and could have an immediate impact' (that is routine work for the PM) and 'a problem that has the potential to affect objectives' (potential means uncertain, which sounds like a risk). The APM definition hinges on TOLERANCES and the SPONSOR.

items: Issue: a problem now breaching, or about to breach, delegated tolerances, needing the sponsor's support to agree a resolution.
It is certain: it has happened or is happening.
Delegated tolerances are the limits within which the PM may act alone.
Problems the PM solves within tolerance are not issues in the APM sense.

summary: You can now define an issue in APM terms and explain the part delegated tolerances and the sponsor play. You can also tell a genuine issue apart from a day-to-day problem the project manager simply resolves.

A.q: Which of the following best defines an issue in APM terms?
options: An uncertain event that could affect the objectives
Any problem the team meets in its daily work
A problem breaching, or about to breach, tolerances
A request to alter the approved project baseline
A.why: An issue is a problem that is breaching, or about to breach, delegated tolerances and needs the sponsor's support to agree a resolution.

whyNot.0: An uncertain event that could affect objectives is a risk.
whyNot.1: Routine problems the PM handles within tolerance are not issues in the APM sense.
whyNot.3: A request to alter the baseline is a change request, handled by change control.

A.q: Whose support is needed to agree the resolution of an issue?
options: The end users
The risk owner
The project team
The project sponsor
A.why: An issue is beyond the PM's delegated tolerances, so the sponsor, who set those tolerances, must support the resolution.

whyNot.0: End users may be affected, but they don't hold the authority to resolve issues.
whyNot.1: Risk owners manage risks, which are uncertain future events, not issues.
whyNot.2: The team carries out actions, but resolving an issue needs authority beyond the PM's.

A.q: What are 'delegated tolerances' on a project?
options: Contingency funds set aside for identified risks
Limits within which the PM may act without escalating
Quality standards that every deliverable must meet
The amount of change the end users will accept
A.why: Delegated tolerances are the permitted deviations (for example in time or cost) within which the project manager can act without going to the sponsor.

whyNot.0: Contingency is a reserve of time or money for risks, not a limit of authority.
whyNot.2: Quality standards define acceptance criteria, not the PM's authority.
whyNot.3: How much change users will accept is a stakeholder concern, not a tolerance.

B.q: A painter is ill for two days, but the project manager recovers the time using float, well within tolerance. In APM terms, this is:
options: an issue, as it has already happened
a day-to-day problem, not an issue
a risk, as it may affect the end date
a change request for the sponsor
B.why: The PM resolved it within delegated tolerance, so it is routine management, not an issue needing the sponsor.

whyNot.0: Having happened is not enough: an issue must also breach, or be about to breach, tolerances.
whyNot.2: It has already happened, so it isn't a risk, and the end date is protected.
whyNot.3: Nothing in the baseline needs to change, so there is no change request.

B.q: A forecast shows the project will exceed its cost tolerance next month, although it has not done so yet. How should this be treated?
options: As an issue, as a breach of tolerance is imminent
As a risk, as the breach has not happened yet
As normal variance for the PM to absorb quietly
As a closed matter until the breach actually occurs
B.why: The APM definition includes problems that are about to breach tolerances. The overspend is already under way, so it should be raised now.

whyNot.1: The problem driving the overspend is real and current; only the breach is still to come, and 'about to breach' is covered by the definition.
whyNot.2: Absorbing it is only possible within tolerance, and this is forecast to exceed it.
whyNot.3: Waiting for the breach removes options the sponsor could have used.

B.q: Which statement about issues is correct?
options: They can be positive as well as negative
They each have a probability of occurring
They are certain: they are happening now
They are handled by the project team only
B.why: An issue has happened or is happening, so it is certain. That is what separates it from a risk.

whyNot.0: Issues are problems. Positive uncertain events are opportunities, which are risks.
whyNot.1: Probability belongs to risks: an issue has already occurred.
whyNot.3: An issue needs the sponsor's support, so it isn't handled by the team alone.

C.q:
Which TWO features must a problem have to count as an issue in APM terms?
1. It has occurred or is occurring.
2. It has a low probability of happening.
3. It breaches, or will soon breach, delegated tolerances.
4. It can be solved by the team without help.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 4
2 and 3
2 and 4
C.why: An issue is a real problem (it has occurred) that breaches or is about to breach delegated tolerances.

whyNot.1: If the team can solve it without help, it is within tolerance and not an issue.
whyNot.2: Probability describes risks; an issue is certain.
whyNot.3: Neither feature fits: issues have no probability and they need the sponsor's support.

C.q: On the Harbourside fit-out, the schedule tolerance is two weeks. The flooring supplier has just collapsed, causing a six-week delay. What should the project manager recognise?
options: A threat to note in the risk register
A minor problem to absorb within float
An opportunity to re-scope the flooring
An issue needing the sponsor's support
C.why: The delay has happened and is three times the delegated tolerance, so it is an issue for the sponsor.

whyNot.0: It is no longer uncertain: the collapse has happened, so it isn't a risk.
whyNot.1: Six weeks far exceeds the two-week tolerance, so it can't be absorbed by the PM.
whyNot.2: This is a problem, not a positive uncertain event.

C.q: Why are tolerances central to the APM definition of an issue?
options: They set the probability score of each issue
They decide whether a problem needs the sponsor
They show which risks have the highest impact
They fix the order of issue resolution stages
C.why: Within tolerance the PM resolves problems; a breach, actual or imminent, is what makes it an issue for the sponsor.

whyNot.0: Issues are certain, so they have no probability score.
whyNot.2: Risk impact is rated in risk analysis, not by tolerances.
whyNot.3: The resolution stages are a fixed process; tolerances don't set their order.

reteach.title: The kitchen refit and the £500 rule
reteach.question: A homeowner tells their builder: 'Fix anything under £500 without asking me; ring me for anything bigger.' How does that one sentence explain what an issue is?

blocks.body: The £500 limit is a delegated tolerance. A cracked tile costing £60? The builder just fixes it: a day-to-day problem. Rotten joists found under the floor costing £2,400? That is beyond the limit, so the builder stops and rings the homeowner, who is acting as the sponsor, to agree what to do. That phone call is an issue being raised.

blocks.text: The tolerance, not how annoying the problem is, decides whether it is an issue. A small but irritating snag within the limit is still the builder's job.

explain.body: An issue is not a 'might'. It has happened or is happening now, so it is certain. That is why it has no probability score: its likelihood is already 100%.

test.q: In what sense is an issue 'certain'?
options: It is sure to happen at a later stage
It has been confirmed by an audit
It has happened or is happening now
It has been approved by the sponsor
test.why: An issue is certain because it has already occurred or is occurring.

whyNot.0: Something expected later is still in the future; an issue is here now.
whyNot.1: Audits are not what makes an issue certain.
whyNot.3: The sponsor helps resolve issues; they don't approve their existence.

explain.body: Delegated tolerances are the limits (for example plus or minus two weeks, or £10,000) within which the PM acts alone. A problem becomes an issue when it breaches them, or is about to.

test.q: A PM's cost tolerance is plus or minus £10,000. Spend is forecast to come in £4,000 over budget. What is this?
options: An issue for the sponsor
A risk to be closed
Within tolerance for the PM
A change to the baseline
test.why: £4,000 is inside the £10,000 tolerance, so the PM handles it without escalating.

whyNot.0: It doesn't breach tolerance, so it isn't an issue.
whyNot.1: It isn't a risk, and nothing needs closing.
whyNot.3: The baseline doesn't change; the PM manages the variance within tolerance.

explain.body: Because the problem is outside the PM's delegated authority, the sponsor, who set the tolerances, must support the resolution. The PM still logs it, assesses it and recommends options.

test.q: Why does an issue need the sponsor's support?
options: The sponsor must personally log every problem
The sponsor carries out all fixing actions
Only the sponsor can score its probability
Its fix is beyond the PM's delegated authority
test.why: An issue breaches the tolerances delegated to the PM, so resolving it needs the authority of the sponsor.

whyNot.0: The PM logs issues, not the sponsor.
whyNot.1: Actions are carried out by the team and suppliers, not the sponsor personally.
whyNot.2: Issues have already happened, so there is no probability to score.

explain.h: Not every problem is an issue
explain.body: Day-to-day problems the PM solves within tolerance are just good management. Calling every hiccup an 'issue' would flood the sponsor and hide the problems that really need them.

rows.label: Permit refused, work halted for months

test.q: Which of the following is NOT an issue in the APM sense?
options: A late delivery fixed within tolerance
A failed test set to breach the end date
A cost overrun now past the tolerance
A refused permit halting work for months
test.why: A problem the PM resolves within tolerance is a day-to-day problem, not an issue.

whyNot.1: A forecast breach of the end-date tolerance makes it an issue.
whyNot.2: An overrun beyond tolerance is a classic issue.
whyNot.3: A halt of months will breach tolerances and need the sponsor.
